system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Representability in Q
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Definitions of a function and a relation being representable in a theory, the equivalence of representable and computable functions in Q, the proof strategy via the basic functions, composition, and regular minimization, and the extension to stronger theories. Excludes the details of the beta function construction and individual Q-derivations.

ATOMS:
- CS-COMP-C03-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A function $f(x_0,\ldots,x_k)$ from the natural numbers to the natural numbers is representable in Q if there is a formula $A_f(x_0,\ldots,x_k,y)$ such that whenever $f(n_0,\ldots,n_k)=m$, Q proves $A_f(\overline{n_0},\ldots,\overline{n_k},\overline{m})$ and Q proves $\forall y\,(A_f(\overline{n_0},\ldots,\overline{n_k},y)\rightarrow \overline{m}=y)$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0095-s01] Definition 4.1. A function f (x0,. . . ,xk) from the natural numbers to the natural numbers is said to be representable in Q if there is a formula Af (x0,. . . ,xk,y) such that whenever f (n0,. . . ,nk) = m, Q proves
- CS-COMP-C03-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: The definition of a function being representable in Q can equivalently require that Q proves $\forall y\,(A_f(\overline{n_0},\ldots,\overline{n_k},y)\leftrightarrow y=\overline{m})$ whenever $f(n_0,\ldots,n_k)=m$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0095-s02] There are other ways of stating the definition; for example, we could equivalently require that Q proves ∀y (Af (n0,. . . ,nk,y) ↔ y = m).
- CS-COMP-C03-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A relation $R(x_0,\ldots,x_k)$ on the natural numbers is representable in Q if there is a formula $A_R(x_0,\ldots,x_k)$ such that Q proves $A_R(\overline{n_0},\ldots,\overline{n_k})$ whenever $R(n_0,\ldots,n_k)$ is true, and Q proves $\neg A_R(\overline{n_0},\ldots,\overline{n_k})$ whenever $R(n_0,\ldots,n_k)$ is false.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0114-s15] Definition 4.28. A relation R(x0,. . . ,xk) on the natural numbers is representable in Q if there is a formula AR(x0,. . . ,xk) such that whenever R(n0,. . . ,nk) is true, Q proves AR(n0,. . . ,nk), and
    [CS-COMP-p0115-s01] whenever R(n0,. . . ,nk) is false, Q proves ¬AR(n0,. . . ,nk).
- CS-COMP-C03-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: A function is representable in Q if and only if it is computable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0095-s03] Theorem 4.2. A function is representable in Q if and only if it is computable.
- CS-COMP-C03-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: A relation is representable in Q if and only if it is computable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0115-s02] Theorem 4.29. A relation is representable in Q if and only if it is computable.
- CS-COMP-C03-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: To show that every computable function is representable in Q, taking computable to mean general recursive, it suffices to show that the basic functions zero, succ, the projections, addition, multiplication and the characteristic function of identity are representable in Q and that functions defined from representable functions by composition or regular minimization are also representable, because every general recursive function can be defined from these basic functions using composition and regular minimization alone.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0114-s02] Consequently, a function is general recursive iff it can be defined from zero, succ, P n i , add, mult, 𝜒= using composition and regular minimization.
    [CS-COMP-p0114-s03] We’ve furthermore shown that the basic functions in question are representable in Q (Propositions 4.10 to 4.13, 4.15 and 4.17), and that any function defined from representable functions by composition or regular minimization (Proposition 4.21, Proposition 4.26) is also representable.
    [CS-COMP-p0114-s04] Thus every general recursive function is representable in Q. □
- CS-COMP-C03-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Any theory extending Q, or in which one can interpret Q, can represent the computable functions.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0114-s07] From the definition of representability, it is not hard to see that any theory extending Q (or in which one can interpret Q) can represent the computable functions.
- CS-COMP-C03-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: In any derivation system in which the notion of derivation is computable, every representable function is computable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0114-s08] But, conversely, in any derivation system in which the notion of derivation is computable, every representable function is computable.
- CS-COMP-C03-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Across a wide range of axiomatic theories the representable functions are exactly the computable ones, so stronger theories than Q do not represent more functions as long as they are axiomatizable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0114-s12] But across a wide range of axiomatic theories, the representable functions are exactly the computable ones; stronger theories do not represent more functions as long as they are axiomatizable.
